::: {.lead}
The studio *Byte Bay* is making *Neon Drift*, a racing game for PCs and
phones. The testers send new reports. "On the phone, the car turns too
sharply." "The laptop shows only 40 frames per second." "The game stutters
on high textures." Each report points to hardware that you have not met yet.
The player steers with an **input device** and sees and hears the race
through **output devices**. Between them, a special processor draws every
frame: the **GPU**, with its own memory. In lecture 3 you met the CPU, the
memory and the storage. In this lesson you describe the devices around them
and the graphics hardware. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary input-device output-device analog-input haptic-feedback gpu parallel-processing frame-rate refresh-rate thermal-throttling video-memory integrated-gpu graphics-card resolution >}}

## 3.1 How the player's action gets into the game

A tester of *Neon Drift* says: "With the keyboard, the car always turns
fully. With the gamepad, I can turn a little." Why do two devices give a
different feeling? Each **input device** turns an action of the player into
numbers. The game reads these numbers in every frame. Different devices
send different kinds of numbers.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 3.1 — Input device"}
An **input device** turns an action of the user (a touch, a key press, a
movement, a sound) into data that the computer can read.
:::

| Input device | The player's action | The numbers the game reads |
|---|---|---|
| touch screen | touch, swipe, pinch | the position of each finger (several at once) |
| keyboard | press a key | which keys are down: on or off |
| mouse | move, click | how far it moved; the buttons on or off |
| gamepad | press buttons, push sticks and triggers | buttons on or off; sticks and triggers as values |
| microphone | speak, blow | the sound level |
| camera | move in front of it | images |

: Common input devices of games (@fig-io). {#tbl-input}

A key or a button is **digital**: it is only on (1) or off (0). A stick or a
trigger is **analog**: it gives any value in a range. A stick gives $-1$
(full left) to $1$ (full right), so the car can turn a little or a lot
(@fig-analog). A touch screen sends the position of every finger. Most phones
can follow several fingers at the same time (multi-touch).

![Input devices send their numbers into the game. Output devices bring the result back to the player.](images/io-devices.png){#fig-io width=94%}

![A key gives 0 or 1. A stick gives any value from −1 to 1.](images/analog-digital.png){#fig-analog width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.1 — Why the keyboard car turns fully"}
In *Neon Drift*, the game turns the car by 40° per second times the input
value.

1. Keyboard: the right arrow is down, so the value is 1. The car turns
   $40 \times 1 = 40°$ per second.
2. Gamepad: the stick is pushed half way right, so the value is 0.5. The car
   turns $40 \times 0.5 = 20°$ per second.
3. The keyboard cannot send 0.5. A keyboard player turns in short taps
   instead.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that every button is analog. On most gamepads, the face buttons
(A, B) are digital. Only the sticks and the triggers are analog.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/input-lab.html" poster="sims/input-lab.png" title="Input Lab: what does the game read?" height="720" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Input Lab"}
Open the **Input Lab** simulator above (or scan its QR code) on your phone.

1. Put one finger on the yellow pad, then two, three… How many fingers does
   your phone follow at once?
2. Drag the on-screen stick half way to the right. Read "stick x". Press A
   and read "button A".

*Your result:* the number of fingers, the stick value, the button value, and
which control is analog.

::: {.check}
A key gives only 0 or 1, so the car turns fully (40° per second) or not at
all. The stick gives values between −1 and 1, so the car can turn a little:
half way gives 20° per second.
:::
:::

## 3.2 How the game talks back: output devices

The race must reach the player's eyes, ears and hands. **Output devices** do
this. The display shows the picture. Speakers or headphones play the sound.
A small **vibration motor** in a phone or a gamepad shakes when the car
crashes: this is **haptic feedback**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 3.2 — Output device"}
An **output device** turns data from the computer into something the user
can see, hear or feel: an image, a sound or a vibration.
:::

Some devices are input and output at the same time (@fig-io). A touch screen
reads fingers and shows the picture. A gamepad has buttons and a vibration
motor. A headset has headphones and a microphone. A device connects to the
computer by a cable (USB, HDMI for a display) or without one (Bluetooth).
The resolution and the refresh rate of the display were in lecture 2.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.2 — The devices of a racing setup"}
A tester plays *Neon Drift* on a PC with a gamepad, a headset and a monitor.

1. Input only: the keyboard and the mouse on the desk.
2. Output only: the monitor.
3. Both: the gamepad (sticks in, vibration out) and the headset (microphone
   in, sound out).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Calling the monitor an input device because it is "connected". The cable
only carries the picture *out* to the player. A normal monitor has no
touch, so it sends nothing into the game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The devices around you"}
On the lab computer, open **Settings → Bluetooth & devices**. On your phone,
look at **Settings → Bluetooth** and at the sound and vibration settings
(Android: **Sound and vibration**; iPhone: **Sounds & Haptics**).

1. List every input and output device of the lab computer and of your phone
   (do not forget the built-in ones: screen, speaker, microphone, cameras).
2. Mark each one "input", "output" or "both".

*Your result:* a table with two columns (lab computer, phone).

::: {.check}
A good list has every device with its kind, for example: keyboard (input),
mouse (input), monitor (output), headset with microphone (both), phone touch
screen (both), phone speaker (output), vibration motor (output).
:::
:::

## 3.3 Why games need a GPU

To draw one frame, the game must compute the colour of every pixel. A
1920 × 1080 screen has about 2 million pixels. At 60 frames per second, that
is about 120 million colours every second. A CPU has a few strong cores
(4 to 16). Each core can run long, different steps, such as the game rules.
But it is too slow for millions of small, similar jobs.

The **GPU** has a different design. It has thousands of small cores
(@fig-cores). Each core is simpler and slower, but they all work at the same
time on different pixels. This is **parallel processing**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 3.3 — Parallel processing"}
**Parallel processing** means doing many small pieces of work at the same
time on many cores, instead of one after another.
:::

![A CPU has a few strong cores. A GPU has thousands of small cores.](images/cpu-gpu-cores.png){#fig-cores width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.3 — The paint race"}
A tiny frame has 16 × 9 = 144 pixels.

1. A CPU with 4 strong cores paints 4 pixels at a time, each in 0.08 s:
   $144 \div 4 = 36$ steps, and $36 \times 0.08 = 2.88$ s.
2. A GPU with 144 small cores paints all pixels at once, each in 0.32 s:
   0.32 s.
3. Each GPU core is 4 times slower, but the whole frame is 9 times faster.
:::

**The GPU and the CPU in every frame.** Every frame needs work from two processors. The **CPU** runs the game logic:
input, rules, movement and the list of things to draw. The **GPU** (graphics
processor) draws the picture: it computes the colour of every pixel. The two
work like an assembly line: while the GPU draws one frame, the CPU already
prepares the next one. So the slower of the two decides the time of each
frame (@fig-pipeline).

![The CPU and the GPU work on two frames at the same time. The slower one sets the pace.](../week-01/images/cpu-gpu-pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=94%}

The **frame rate** is the number of new pictures that the game makes per
second (frames per second, fps). The **refresh rate** is the number of times
per second that the screen redraws its picture (60, 90 or 120 Hz). The
**resolution** is the number of pixels: width × height. More pixels mean more
work for the GPU. The player never sees more new pictures than the slower of
the two rates allows: a game at 70 fps on a 60 Hz screen shows 60 new pictures
per second.

A phone has no fan. After some minutes of heavy play, the chip gets hot. To
protect itself, the phone slows the processor down. This is called **thermal
throttling**. A game that runs at 60 fps in the first minute may drop to 40
fps after twenty minutes. So developers test games for a long time, not only
for one minute.


::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The GPU is a faster CPU." It is not. A GPU core is slower than a CPU core.
The GPU wins only when the work splits into many similar pieces, like
pixels. The game rules still run on the CPU.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/paint-race.html" poster="sims/paint-race.png" title="Paint Race: CPU or GPU?" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Paint Race"}
Open the **Paint Race** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Press **Start the race**. Write the two times.
2. Explain in one sentence why the GPU wins, although each of its cores is
   slower.

*Your result:* two times and your sentence.

::: {.check}
The CPU (4 cores) takes about 2.88 s, the GPU (144 cores) about 0.32 s. The
GPU wins because all its small cores colour different pixels at the same
time.
:::
:::

## 3.4 Video memory and graphics settings

A tester reports: "On high textures, the laptop stutters." The GPU keeps the
textures of the game and the frames it draws in **video memory** (VRAM).
There are two designs (@fig-vram):

- An **integrated GPU** is part of the processor chip, as in most laptops
  and all phones. It has no memory of its own. It takes part of the main RAM
  (for example 2 GB).
- A **graphics card** has its own GPU and its own fast video memory (for
  example 8 GB). Gaming desktops have one.

If the textures do not fit into the video memory, the GPU must keep moving
them in and out. The game stutters.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 3.4 — Video memory"}
**Video memory** (VRAM) is the memory that the GPU uses for textures and
frames. A graphics card has its own. An integrated GPU shares the main RAM.
:::

![Integrated GPU: CPU and GPU share the RAM. Graphics card: the GPU has its own VRAM.](images/gpu-memory.png){#fig-vram width=94%}

The **graphics settings** of a game change the work of the GPU (@tbl-settings).

| Setting | What it changes | Effect on the GPU |
|---|---|---|
| resolution | the number of pixels in each frame | 1080p has about twice the pixels of 720p: about half the frame rate |
| texture quality | the size of the textures | higher textures need more video memory |
| shadows and effects | extra work for every pixel | the frame rate drops |

: Three common graphics settings. {#tbl-settings}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.4 — Settings for a tablet"}
A puzzle game runs at 150 fps on a tablet at 720p with shadows off. The
tablet has an integrated GPU with 1 GB of video memory. The goal is 60 fps.

1. 1080p doubles the pixels: about $150 \div 2 = 75$ fps. Enough.
2. 1080p with shadows on: $75 \div 1.5 = 50$ fps. Too slow.
3. Medium textures need 2 GB, but the tablet has 1 GB: they do not fit. Low
   textures (1 GB) fit.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The GPU of the lab computer"}
On a lab computer, open **Task Manager** (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) **→ Performance
→ GPU 0**.

1. Write the name of the GPU.
2. Write the **Dedicated GPU memory** and the **Shared GPU memory**.
3. Is it an integrated GPU or a graphics card? Give your reason.

*Your result:* three lines.

::: {.check}
A typical lab computer shows an Intel or AMD GPU with a small dedicated
memory and a large shared memory: an integrated GPU, because it shares the
main RAM. A graphics card shows several GB of dedicated GPU memory.
:::
:::

## Case study: tuning Neon Drift

*Neon Drift* must run at 60 fps or more on three test devices of *Byte Bay*.
In this made-up game, the frame rate follows two simple rules: 1080p halves
the frame rate of 720p, and shadows divide it by 1.5. The textures need 1 GB
(Low), 2 GB (Medium) or 4 GB (High) of video memory.

- **Laptop L1:** GPU inside the processor, 2 GB of video memory; 120 fps at
  720p with shadows off.
- **Phone P1:** GPU inside the chipset, 2 GB of video memory; 90 fps at
  720p with shadows off.
- **Desktop D1:** graphics card with 8 GB of VRAM; 300 fps at 720p with
  shadows off.

The tester must choose settings that reach 60 fps and fit into the video
memory of each device. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these numbers. In the mini-game below you tune the three devices.

{{< sim file="sims/settings-tuner.html" poster="sims/settings-tuner.png" title="Settings Tuner: Neon Drift on three devices" kind="game" height="760" >}}

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 2,
the sections on input/output devices (keyboards, mice, displays) and on
graphics processors.

## Exercises

1. Name two input devices and two output devices of a phone.
2. Name a device that is input and output at the same time. Explain why.
3. What is the difference between a digital and an analog input? Give one
   example of each.
4. A stick is pushed fully to the left. Which value does the game read?
5. What is haptic feedback? Give one example in a game.
6. Why does a GPU have thousands of small cores instead of a few strong ones?
7. Where does an integrated GPU keep its textures?
8. A game needs 3 GB of video memory for high textures. A laptop has an
   integrated GPU with 2 GB. What happens? What can the player do?
9. *Neon Drift* runs at 90 fps at 720p on Phone P1. About how many fps does it
   reach at 1080p? Is it enough?
10. Which device of *Byte Bay* can use high textures (4 GB)? Why?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Input: touch screen, microphone, camera. Output: display, speaker, vibration motor.
2. For example a touch screen: it reads touches (input) and shows the picture (output). Or a gamepad with vibration, or a headset.
3. Digital: only on or off (a key, the A button). Analog: a range of values (a stick, a trigger).
4. −1.
5. Output that the player feels as a touch, for example the gamepad shakes when the car crashes.
6. Each pixel needs a small, similar job, and there are millions of pixels. Many small cores do them at the same time (parallel processing).
7. In the main RAM, which it shares with the CPU.
8. The textures do not fit, so the game stutters. The player can choose lower textures.
9. About 90 ÷ 2 = 45 fps. No, it is less than 60.
10. Desktop D1: its graphics card has 8 GB of VRAM. L1 and P1 have only 2 GB.
:::
